physical_harm: Death of the child caused by acid burns
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation as the acid was obtained and used to kill the child
motive: To get rid of the child so that she could not claim any share in her father's property
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that nitric and sulphuric acids were obtained from PW.17 and mixed into a concoction that was put into the mouth of the child, based on medical evidence showing injuries across the body indicating the child fought back against the acid administration.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the prosecution's witnesses, noting discrepancies in their statements and doubting the truthfulness of the prosecution's story, but ultimately found the High Court's re-evaluation of the evidence to be justified.
post_offence_conduct: The appellant absconded after the incident and was arrested later.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 22nd September 1996; Trial judgment: 28th April 1999; High Court decision: Not stated; Supreme Court decision: July 28, 2010
legal_representation: Ajit Kumar Panda (for the Appellant); Ramesh Kumar Mishra, K. Joshi, Ramesh S. Jadhav and Vikrant Yadav (for the Respondent)
investigation_status: FIR lodged by Jayanthi PW.1; charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Acquittal; High Court: Set aside acquittal of appellant No.1, convicted under Section 302; Supreme Court: Appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant and the co-accused intentionally administered nitric and sulphuric acid to the child Pallavi, leading to her death, and that the Trial Court's acquittal was based on incorrect interpretation of the evidence.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the Trial Court's acquittal was justified as there were two possible views on the evidence, and the High Court's interference was unwarranted unless the Trial Court's judgment was perverse.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that if two views are possible and the Trial Court has recorded an acquittal, the High Court should not interfere unless the Trial Court's view was not based on the evidence and would defeat the ends of justice.
sentencing_rationale: The High Court's conviction and sentencing of the appellant under Section 302 of the IPC was based on the evidence that the acid was forcibly administered to the child, leading to her death, and the Trial Court's view was found to be unjustified.
